claims.text: The initial Mg-containing lightweight alloy is in a non-equilibrium, metastable solid-solution-containing state.
Rapid solidification or initial ball milling can produce the stated metastable solid-solution-containing initial state.
Ball milling followed by SPS can produce a multiphase Mg-containing multi-principal-element alloy.
A controlled SPS heating profile will transform the metastable solid solution into finely and uniformly dispersed intermetallic precipitates.
Optimizing SPS dwell time and temperature will tune the kinetics of the metastable-to-equilibrium transformation and intermetallic precipitation.
Fine intermetallic precipitates act as nucleation sites and stabilizers for a coherent, continuous protective oxide layer.
A continuous and adherent protective scale resists spallation and maintains corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance.
The controlled thermal profile moderates diffusion rates and nucleation kinetics, limiting intermetallic formation and distributing it uniformly.
Uncontrolled heating promotes coarse, unevenly distributed or segregated intermetallic phases.
Coarse intermetallics create stress concentrations and disrupt the passive or oxide film.
SPS near 1050 °C with a short dwell can achieve rapid densification while avoiding extensive grain growth or coarsening.
The controlled process will produce finer intermetallic precipitates than both the initial metastable state and the uncontrolled-sintering baseline.
The controlled process will produce a more intact and coherent passive film than the initial state and uncontrolled-sintering baseline.
The controlled process will reduce oxidation mass gain at 900 °C relative to the baseline.
The controlled process will improve corrosion performance, as indicated by a higher corrosion potential and lower corrosion current density.
The proposed mechanism applies around 900 °C in air and during immersion in 3.5% NaCl.
Minor deviations in Mg content may alter intermetallic nucleation rates.
Failure to obtain statistically finer, more uniform precipitates together with improved oxidation and corrosion performance relative to the conventional baseline would falsify the hypothesis.
